cim: Beyond detection: How artificial intelligence is transforming clinical dental hygiene practice
cim_eredeti: Beyond detection: How artificial intelligence is transforming clinical dental hygiene practice
szoveg_eredeti:
Every day, dental hygienists make hundreds of clinical decisions that influence patient outcomes—from recognizing subtle radiographic changes to determining appropriate periodontal therapy and educating patients about their oral health. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into dental practice, it offers an opportunity to support these decisions through enhanced radiographic interpretation, improved documentation, and more meaningful patient communication.

For dental hygienists, AI is far more than a technology trend. It is an emerging clinical tool that can improve diagnostic consistency, streamline workflows, and support patient-centered care. By transforming complex clinical findings into clear, visual information, AI can facilitate codiagnosis, improve treatment acceptance, and reinforce evidence-based clinical decision-making.

While AI continues to evolve rapidly, its greatest value lies not in replacing clinical expertise, but in enhancing it. The dental hygienist remains responsible for interpreting findings within the context of the patient's clinical presentation, risk factors, and overall health. When thoughtfully integrated into practice, AI has the potential to elevate—not replace—the clinician's judgment while improving consistency across the dental team.

AI is changing the way clinicians interpret radiographs and identify periodontal disease. Advanced imaging platforms can detect subtle changes in crestal bone height, quantify radiographic bone loss, and compare findings over time with a level of consistency that may be difficult to achieve through visual interpretation alone. For dental hygienists, these technologies provide an additional layer of clinical information that supports earlier recognition of periodontal breakdown and more confident treatment planning.

However, AI should never be viewed as a substitute for comprehensive periodontal assessment. Radiographic findings represent only one component of diagnosis. Accurate classification still depends on clinical attachment level (CAL), probing depths, bleeding on probing, recession, furcation involvement, mobility, medical history, and an understanding of disease activity.1 AI can identify patterns and highlight areas of concern, but it cannot independently determine etiology, classify disease, or establish an individualized treatment plan.

The true strength of AI lies in supporting clinical reasoning. By combining enhanced radiographic interpretation with comprehensive periodontal assessment, dental hygienists can improve diagnostic consistency, facilitate earlier intervention, and provide patients with a clearer understanding of their periodontal health. Rather than replacing the clinician, AI serves as another piece of the diagnostic puzzle—one that helps translate data into more informed clinical decisions.2

AI identifies findings. Dental hygienists integrate those findings with clinical evidence to make informed diagnostic and treatment decisions (figures 1 and 2).

Figure 1: CALibrate™ Clinical Decision Pathway: Integrating artificial intelligence into periodontal assessment and treatment planning. Artificial intelligence adds the significant advantage of longitudinal monitoring, but is limited in providing an accurate baseline due to the inability to interpret a coronal margin vs. recession. Comprehensive periodontal assessment, classification, patient education, treatment planning, and clinical judgement remain the responsibility of the dental hygienist.

Figure 2: Artificial intelligence-assisted radiographic assessment of interproximal bone levels on a posterior bitewing radiograph. The software identifies the cementoenamel junction (CEJ), alveolar crest, and interproximal bone level to calculate radiographic bone loss while highlighting restorations and other radiographic findings.

AI does more than identify disease—it changes how clinicians communicate it. For decades, dental hygienists have relied on radiographs, periodontal charting, and intraoral photographs to explain disease progression and justify treatment recommendations. While these tools remain essential, many patients struggle to understand the relationship between what they see on an image and what it means for their long-term oral health.

AI bridges this communication gap by converting complex diagnostic information into clear, visual representations that are easier for patients to understand. Color overlays, highlighted areas of bone loss, and side-by-side comparisons of previous radiographs transform abstract findings into meaningful conversations. Rather than simply telling patients they have periodontal disease, clinicians can show them exactly where changes have occurred and how those findings support treatment recommendations.

This visual approach encourages codiagnosis, allowing patients to become active participants in their care rather than passive recipients of information. When patients better understand the relationship between biofilm, inflammation, attachment loss, and bone destruction, they are often more receptive to preventive recommendations and periodontal therapy.3 AI does not replace the clinician's ability to educate—it enhances the conversation by making clinical findings more tangible and easier to comprehend.

Ultimately, technology supports what dental hygienists have always done best: educate, motivate, and empower patients to make informed decisions about their oral health.

Patients are more likely to accept treatment when they understand what clinicians see (table 1).

Artificial intelligence is most effective when integrated throughout the entire patient appointment—from assessment and education to treatment planning and long-term periodontal maintenance.

Complete and accurate documentation remains one of the cornerstones of periodontal care. Yet studies continue to demonstrate significant variability in periodontal charting and documentation among clinicians, with less than 16% of periodontal charts recorded to completion. Incomplete records may affect diagnostic consistency, treatment planning, communication among providers, and insurance reimbursement.

AI, particularly when combined with voice-assisted periodontal charting and integrated practice management systems, offers an opportunity to improve both efficiency and consistency. Voice documentation captures probing depths, recession, bleeding on probing, furcation involvement, mobility, and other clinical findings. When bleeding on probing affects 30% or more of the mouth, it is consistent with generalized moderate gingivitis. Often, concerns regarding insurance coverage and reimbursement will limit the use of the preventive CDT code 4346 for scaling in the presence of generalized moderate to severe gingival inflammation.

More importantly, AI can aggregate information from multiple sources—including periodontal charting, radiographs, intraoral images, and previous examinations—to present clinicians with a comprehensive view of periodontal health. This longitudinal perspective helps identify trends that may not be immediately apparent during a single appointment, supporting earlier intervention and more informed clinical decision-making.4 Images with AI-assisted radiographic interpretation, along with comprehensive depiction of CAL and disease activity, will support early coverage for D4341 and D4342, nonsurgical scaling and root planing.

Improved documentation also benefits communication with insurance carriers. Thorough clinical records, supported by radiographic findings and objective measurements, strengthen documentation for appropriate coding and reimbursement when periodontal therapy is indicated.5 While AI does not determine treatment or coding, it can help ensure that the supporting clinical evidence is organized, complete, and readily accessible. This enables timelier intervention, preserving supportive structures, and improving long-term patient outcomes.
